I may be an older dude for the voat demographic, over 40, but I can tell you the difference in the world now vs 1994 is marked and incredible. Before the internet we had only conventional media for news and had to rely on the facts and opinions being broadcasted to us. There were issues going on in the world that we would never be told about, because it was deemed to not be relevant or captivating enough to take up time in the 1 hour newscast or "not worth the ink" in the papers. If you were so inclined, you could take a trip to the local library and check out some international newspapers and magazines, but then even still you were getting usually only 1 side of the story.

Today, I can access news from across the world with a click. And not only that, I can watch videos produced by real people living lives that I would never have imagined. And, through communities like Voat I can have unfiltered conversations with real people from anywhere and everywhere around the world.

The internet was and continues to be the greatest communication tool mankind has ever created. The revolution that was the beginning of the Information Age saw the consumer become the agent of control of the information which he consumed. No longer would information be "pushed" out to the masses, now it is "pulled" and I have the freedom of choice to research and learn as much or as little as I wanted, about even controversial opinions and viewpoints that would never be presented to me (the Palestinian / Israeli conflict, Tibet, and much more) - in the past, outside of me getting on an airplane and going out to see for myself, there was no alternative.

Consider that I could go onto facebook, twitter, or /v/france (or that other place) and get real-time updates from real citizens on the street living in France during the Charlie Hebdo attack and be able to read and understand the posts there in French because I had learned French from taking free lessons on the internet. It's an incredible age that we live in, right now.

I intensely love the fact that, through the internet, you can find the kind of people you want to socialise with. Nothing about the internet obliges you to limit your interaction with them to online-only, either.

Internet interaction can be anonymous to whatever degree suits you, allowing you to speak more openly about personal matters than in any other arena, or to make an offering of yourself to potential lovers, employers, friends, whatever.

You can find people to agree with you or educate you in things you already partly agree with, or you can find people to spar with. Personally, doing so has improved my mind and taught me far more patience and consideration.

You can gather intelligence on things you want to know about, at a lower risk and expense than ever before. You can turn on fascinating video or text content, and drop it without a moment's thought if it ceases to suit you.

You can have information routinely sent to you by things like RSS, and companies are constantly finding ways to better tailor what is sent to you. You can have tailored advertising, and companies want to advertise to you in the most tailored way.

Any time you need a LOL, you can find one. Ditto beautiful pictures or stories that touch you emotionally. You can find reams of free advice and thousands of free games and other kinds of entertainment. You can educate yourself to university standard and beyond, in loads of subjects, for free. You can just ask 'the world' a question and have loads of answers in minutes.

Kids who have a birthday coming up and no friends to come to their parties sometimes find a crowd of loving people turning up to transform their world, cos they heard about it on the internet. Man, that makes me cry at the beauty of it.

News and the general exchange of information are becoming ever more p2p. I remember the Boston bombings breaking on Twitter and watching Sky News at the same time. Sky News was a complete joke in comparison - slow, censored, repetitive, cliched.

There's cryptocurrencies and blockchain technology in general. p2p lending. Incredible strides in convenience. Internet shopping. Ever greater consumer standards expected of, and met, by evolving, responsive organisations.

These are magnificent things IMO. You choose your own duration, intensity and character of involvement. Nothing else in human history, it seems to me, compares to the freedom and bounty that the internet permits.

If what I've said seems partly irrelevant to the question - no, my point is that all of these things are extensions of the idea of free, consensual association. Gradually, though perhaps relatively rapidly, we are re-forming our lives around what we as individuals want from one another, thanks in great part to the internet.

If it makes you further apart from anyone, it probably just helps you realise that you're alienated from, or incompatible with, that person already.

I find redeeming qualities in the first Bioshock, second one be damned, that I just don't see in Infinite. The set pieces in infinite were pretty, but I don't think they set atmosphere well beyond that first moment when you arrive in Columbia. Several moments in the first installment painted utopia gone awry remarkably well and there was something to be said of the loneliness in #1. I came to think of myself as a lone bastion of sanity awash in all this libertine disassociation. Of course, you find out everyone in that damn bubble is nuts.

But, yes, it's game play is still limited to a very linear path and you do seem to fight, I can think of 6, different enemies who are just re-costumed and spat back out in different locales. Dear god. I just realized that's exactly what infinite is: the same exact challenge in a different location. With the exception of an even more contrived "twisty" plot, it's game play is just BioShock redressed with more insistently displayed breasts. I did not play the DLC because I just had so much hate for Infinite, but I mean, they even set one of those in Rapture. I think I just felt my liver burst.

The rapture DLC is quite possibly one of my favorite "games". You weren't forced to kill anyone, the story was really good, and it really emotionally connected me with Elizabeth. The first part was meh ok, the second part blew me away. It was still pretty linear, however if you attempt to sneak through without killing a single person it's quite a fun go.
Reviews I read state that it's actually challenging, which is a far cry from the dreck of the core game. I may have to give this one a shot.

Sonic 2006, and for that matter, nearly all Sonic games, have absolutely beautiful soundtracks.

This is something that SEGA have never failed at. They have such a talented sound design studio, and close ties with Tokyo Philharmonic Orchestra.
What ABOUT Sonic R? Sonic R had a fantastic Eurodance soundtrack.
Heavenly sword. Beautiful sound track. Amazing cut scenes. The fighting system was ass.

I was not particularly fond of FFX, but holy man did I play the shit out of Blitzball in that game. It's basically all I did, I would only advance the story if it was necessary to move on with Blitzball. I had a problem.

Brothers: a tale of two sons, I thought the controls were awful for this game and the story was just trying so hard to be sad and it wasn't. However I liked how the world itself look and had a lot of beautiful environment, plus the shadows were really good.

I never really liked the Donkey Kong Country games (SNES); I think that they're overly-detailed for the limited graphics of the time. That said, my brother and I still play it from time to time simply because the co-op is pretty nicely implemented. Unlike a lot of "take turns co-op" games of the era, in DKC you play until you die and then the game immediately switches to Player 2 to pick up where you left off. It's pretty satisfying to get part of the way through, die in some completely unexpected manner, and then your co-op buddy takes the torch and runs with it to complete the level.

Halo 4 I thought was horrible. Plot sucked, those online mini games were bad

Loved the Star Fox level at the end though :)
The mech was totally imbalanced and fun as fuck too, also wrecking people with it online was awesome. The story did suck ass, but I thought the rest of the game was allright.
The mo-cap and voice acting are good in the Uncharted series.

Final Fantasy XIII had a decent (if confusing) story, and a spectacular battle system. I loved having to treat the entire party as a single tactical unit rather than micromanaging each character's individual action; it felt like being a commander on a battlefield rather than a player ordering each action. The fast pace was a welcome change from many RPGs too. It's just to bad that the utterly mind-numbing level design and repetitive enemies kept me from wanting to finish the game despite enjoying the battle system.
